study.title: 2 Kings 6 - Elisha, the deliverance and the crisis in Samaria
study.overview: The chapter gathers signs of God's care through Elisha in very different situations: simple material need, strategic information in wartime, deliverance of the prophet before a siege and, finally, the extreme misery of Samaria under enemy blockade. The text shows that the prophet serves both the sons of the prophets and the king, and that the word of the LORD rules both the secret of men and the national despair. At the same time, the chapter ends in tension: the city is in ruin, the king attributes calamity to the Lord and seems to lose hope of immediate help.

outline.title: The community of prophets and the lost axe
outline.explanation: The sons of the prophets ask for greater space to live and work near the Jordan. During the cutting of wood, one of them loses a sprinted axe in the water; Elisha intervenes and the object floats again, preserving something valuable and relieving man's distress.

outline.title: Elisha frustrates Syria and frees his enemies
outline.explanation: The king of Syria plans ambushes, but Elisha reveals to the king of Israel the enemy military movements. When Syria tries to capture Elisha in Dothan, the prophet prays, the eyes of the servant are opened to see the heavenly army, and the Syrians themselves are led to Samaria. Elisha prevents them from being killed and sends them away after food and drink, which temporarily interrupts Syrian incursions.

outline.title: The Siege of Samaria and the despair of the king
outline.explanation: Ben-Hadade surrounds Samaria and causes extreme hunger, with absurd prices and the collapse of social life. A woman reports to the king a terrible case of cannibalism during famine. The king reacts with lamentation, wears a sackcloth underneath and decides to seek Elisha's head, while the prophet notices the threat before the messenger arrived.

study.context: The notes indicate that the scenery involves the region of the Jordan, near Jericho and Gilgal, where there was wood for construction, and also Dothan and Samaria. Matthew Henry understands that the house of the sons of the prophets was in Gilgal, near the Jordan, and that his number grew. The notes also show that the siege of Samaria led to a severe famine, comparable to the judgment announced in the Law and reminded by the commentators as a time of extreme desolation. There is no basis for notes to add geographic or chronological details beyond these.
study.theology: The chapter highlights God's sovereignty over small and large needs. The sinking axe shows that the Lord cares about a borrowed good and the affliction of a servant. The revelation of the Syrian plans teaches that no secret counsel escapes divine knowledge, and that the prophetic vocation includes serving the people and the king. The vision of fire cars shows that the invisible reality is greater than the visible threat. The merciful treatment of the defeated Syrians teaches that victory should not be used for cruelty. Finally, the hunger in Samaria and the king's crisis show that divine discipline can expose human guilt, but the text does not allow to conclude that every specific calamity is explained in a simple and direct way. The king's speech in verse 33 expresses dismay and perhaps resignation, as the chapter prepares the divine intervention that will come next.

scholarViews.insight: Iron was valuable at that time, and as the axe was borrowed, the loss became even more painful for the man who used it.
The number of disciples increased to the point of lack of space, which is seen as a good sign of the growth of the school of prophets under the influence of Elisha.
The king of Syria was reckless not to consider that Elisha, who had already penetrated his military secrets, could also know his machinations against his own life.

questions: What does the healing of the lost ax teach about God's interest in the small and concrete needs of his people?
How does Elisha's prayer change the way to see the conflict between the Syrian army and the people of God?
How does Elisha's response to the Syrians contrast with the reaction of the king of Israel to the crisis of Samaria?
study.practice: This chapter invites the reader to trust in God in the common losses, public threats and crises that seem to be left. In practice, it is worth asking for spiritual eyes to realize that the reality of God is greater than fear, acting with mercy instead of revenge when one has an advantage over the enemy, and avoid interpreting suffering only by the emotion of the moment. It is also a call to value the presence of servants of God who instruct, correct and sustain the people in times of pressure.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not allow to safely state whether the narrator of verse 33 is the king, the messenger or Elisha himself; the commentators differ in this regard. There is also no basis on the notes to detail exact dates, authors, nor to expand geography beyond Jordan, Dothan, Samaria, Jericho and Gilgal mentioned or inferred in the notes. The division between this chapter and the following, mentioned by Adam Clarke, is an editorial remark, not a decisive conclusion on the content of the text.
